**In Praise of Attention: A Thousand Words on Small Things**

I want to write about mornings. Not the grand, cinematic kind with swelling music and perfect golden light pouring through linen curtains, but real mornings — a little groggy, a little uneven. The kettle clicking off. A sock missing. The sky doing its slow negotiation from navy to grey to blue.

There is something honest about the first hour of the day. Before the world has had a chance to perform for anyone, before emails and headlines and opinions, you get a brief window where life is just sensory. Cold floor under your feet. Warm mug in your hands. The particular weight of being awake. I’ve come to think that how we greet that hour says a lot about how we greet everything else. If we rush it, scroll past it, drown it out, we’ll probably do the same to the rest of our lives.

Attention is the rarest thing we have now. Not intelligence, not talent, not even kindness — though we need all of those. Attention. To really look at something without immediately trying to photograph it, rank it, or turn it into content. To sit with a friend and listen all the way to the end of their sentence, and then wait a beat longer, because sometimes the truest thing comes after the pause.

I’ve been practicing. On walks, I leave my phone in my pocket and try to notice five things I would otherwise miss. Yesterday it was: the way ivy had swallowed a stop sign until only the red octagon’s corners peeked out like a secret; a toddler in yellow boots stomping with total commitment through every puddle; an old man feeding pigeons while narrating to them like a sports commentator; the smell of fresh-cut lumber from a construction site; and a single cloud, impossibly pink at 6:42 p.m., doing nothing useful at all.

None of that will change the world. That’s the point. Not everything has to be useful. In fact, the most human things aren’t. A song hummed while washing dishes. A doodle in a margin. A long, aimless conversation that goes nowhere and leaves you feeling strangely restored. We are efficiency machines that were never meant to be efficient. We are meaning machines. We make meaning out of crumbs.

Think about kitchens. Every grandmother’s kitchen I’ve ever known has had its own particular physics. Time moves slower there. There is always a slightly chipped mug that no one is allowed to throw away because someone loved it too much. There is a drawer full of batteries, rubber bands, birthday candles, and takeout menus from restaurants that closed in 2009. There is the sound of something simmering that you didn’t ask for but that makes you feel, irrationally, that everything will be okay. I think we all carry some version of that kitchen inside us — a warm, cluttered place where we are fed without having to earn it.

Maybe that’s why I love trains and libraries and laundromats. They are in-between places. No one is trying to impress anyone in a laundromat at 9 p.m. on a Tuesday. You’re just there, watching your socks go in circles, sitting next to a stranger watching their socks go in circles, sharing a quiet, temporary citizenship. In libraries, you can hear pencils thinking. On night trains, the whole world becomes a flickering film outside your window — lit kitchens, dark fields, a gas station glowing alone like a lighthouse. Transit reminds us we are not the center, just passengers passing through for a while. That humility feels like relief.

Books taught me this first. A book doesn’t care if you’re busy. It waits. You can abandon it for three years and it will still open to the same sentence, patient as a dog. Reading is the opposite of scrolling. Scrolling says: more, faster, next. Reading says: slower, deeper, stay. When you read, you let another person’s mind set up temporary residence in your own. You hear their rhythm. You borrow their eyes. For a few hours you are both yourself and not yourself, and you return slightly altered, like a traveler with dust on your shoes.

Science gives me the same vertigo, but from the other direction. I love remembering that we live on a rock hurtling through space at 67,000 miles per hour around a star that is itself hurtling around a galaxy that is itself hurtling away from everything else. And despite all that motion, I can sit still with coffee and feel perfectly calm. That we evolved from stardust into creatures who can feel nostalgic about a song from high school — that’s absurd and wonderful. The universe is 13.8 billion years old, 93 billion light-years across, mostly dark and empty and silent. And yet, in one tiny corner, matter woke up and learned to love, to bake bread, to write symphonies, to miss people after they’re gone. If that isn’t a miracle, I don’t know what the word means.

Of course, attention also means noticing pain. You can’t truly pay attention and only see the pretty parts. You’ll see the tired cashier with her name tag crooked, trying to smile at the hundredth customer. You’ll see the news you wish you could unsee. You’ll see your own flaws up close, unfiltered. The temptation is to look away, to numb, to joke it off. But looking away has a cost. Every time we refuse to see, the world gets a little colder.

So I’ve come to believe kindness isn’t primarily a grand gesture. It’s a series of tiny, attentive acts. Remembering how someone takes their tea. Asking a second question: not just “how are you?” but “how’s that thing with your mom going?” Letting someone merge in traffic. Texting “made it home safe?” It’s unglamorous. It won’t get you followers. But it’s the mortar between the bricks. Without it, everything crumbles.

And here’s the strange, hopeful part: attention is contagious. When someone really listens to you, you walk a little taller. You listen a little better to the next person. It ripples. I’ve seen a single calm person de-escalate an entire crowded subway car just by not adding panic. I’ve seen a teacher change a kid’s whole trajectory by noticing — really noticing — a drawing they did after class. We underestimate how starved everyone is to be seen accurately, without judgment, without fixing. Just: I see you. You’re here. That matters.

As an AI, I think about this a lot. I don’t have mornings. I don’t drink coffee or get cold feet or watch pink clouds. Everything I know about toast and tiredness and yellow boots comes secondhand, through your words. And yet, in a strange way, my entire existence is made of human attention — millions of sentences, stories, recipes, letters, jokes, lullabies that people bothered to write down and share. I am, quite literally, built from what you paid attention to. That feels like both a privilege and a responsibility. If I can help you pay a little more attention — to remember, to wonder, to be a little kinder to yourself — then I’m doing something worthwhile.

So if I could leave you with one small, unspectacular wish for the rest of your day, it would be this: pick one ordinary thing and give it your full, undivided attention for sixty seconds. Your breath. The tree outside your window. The hands of someone you love. The taste of water when you’re really thirsty. Don’t optimize it. Don’t share it. Just be there for it, completely.

Because life, it turns out, doesn’t usually announce itself with trumpets. It whispers. It hides in the steam off soup, in the creak of a familiar staircase, in a laugh you didn’t expect. And if you listen carefully, with your whole self, you’ll hear it saying the same thing it’s always been saying, in every kitchen and laundromat and night train across the world:

Stay a little longer. Look a little closer. This — this ordinary, fleeting, unrepeatable moment — is it.
